newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Focus - Russia presses on with spending cut plans.
newsitem.headline: Focus - Russia presses on with spending cut plans.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin urged parliament on Wednesday to back plans to slash spending across the board and said his government would not give in to the inflationary temptation to print more cash.

Chernomyrdin, reviewing the Russian economy in the first quarter of this year, said there were signs of growth in several sectors. Budget revenues had improved in March and April, but spending was still too high.

"The situation in March and April has improved somewhat, but this is still not conclusive," Chernomyrdin told the State Duma lower house of parliament. "We have no reason to hope that the situation will improve by itself."
Chernomyrdin is bound to face a rocky ride from deputies in parliament, which is dominated by communists and their conservative allies.

He had been expected to spend the whole day in parliament, but Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov told deputies that Chernomyrdin and his two first deputies were being summoned to an unexpected meeting in the Kremlin.
A Kremlin spokesman could not say why President Boris Yeltsin wanted to see his ministers so urgently.

Even the small group of liberals in the parliament is bitter at government action and Grigory Yavlinsky, who heads the Duma's Yabloko group, told reporters he had collected 93 signatures calling for a vote of no-confidence in the government.

Under Duma rules, such a vote must be put on the agenda within seven days if more than 90 deputies call for it but most of the deputies, including the communists, have indicated they did not want to topple the government.

The liberals and the conservatives have suggested different routes to tackle Russia's economic crisis, where dismal tax revenues and poor budget discipline have created a web of non-payments which leaves millions below the poverty line.
Some communist deputies have suggested doubling money supply to provide companies and the government with the cash they need to pay overdue bills.
Chernomyrdin said the government would never agree to this.
"The government and above all the central bank are carrying out a policy to control monetary emission which is aimed at lowering interest rates," he said.

The prime minister, now taking something of a back seat to reformers Anatoly Chubais and Anatoly Nemtsov, said a large increase in money supply would re-ignite inflation, widen the budget deficit and cause the rouble to crash.
Western economists see sharply lower inflation as Russia's biggest economic achievement since the country launched a market-oriented reform programme in January 1992.

Consumer prices are expected to rise 12 percent this year, just over half the level seen in 1996. Economic output is expected to stay flat although some sectors -- notably machine building, oil and light industry -- are already growing.
Chernomyrdin said the government had overestimated its ability to collect taxes and now needed to sequester funds -- cut spending for all but the most essential services.

"The government has not been able to do everything which was planned, specifically improving tax collection... We have overestimated our possibility to mobilise incomes... The budget includes 30 trillion roubles ($5.2 billion) which were supposed to come from new taxes.
"All that dictates the need to sequester the budget."
Chernomyrdin said revenues in the first four months of this year were only 64.6 percent of budgeted levels, while expenditure was 70 percent of plan.
The 1997 budget says the government must propose spending cuts to the Duma if revenues fall below 90 percent of budgeted levels in any quarter.
The government now wants to cut 108 trillion roubles from spending levels outlined in the "unrealistic" 1997 budget. Deputies are due to vote on the proposal on Friday. ($ = 5748 Russian Roubles)
